progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From c13: the reaction map; the four moves (name and count, work backwards, choose, write forwards and check); "work backwards to plan, write forwards to answer"; the main road from ethene; the haloalkane side road; dead end; intermediate; overall yield. From c04a: an unsymmetrical alkene can give two products, a symmetrical one gives one; water or HX on propene goes mainly to the middle carbon. From c04b: UV substitution gives a mixture. From c06: hydroxide takes the halogen's place on the same carbon. From c08a: the class rule (primary to aldehyde or acid, secondary to ketone, tertiary no reaction); distil against reflux; [O]; orange to green. From c08b: ketone names with locants (hexan-2-one, hexan-3-one). From c10: the ester cut at the single-bonded O; naming order (alkyl first, then "-oate"); ⇌; keeping a portion of an alcohol back. From c01: numbering carbons; isomers (same formula, different structure).
progression.startsWith: An unseen target with two possible starting materials. The video opens: A synthesis question gives you a target and a short list of things you're allowed to start from.
progression.stopsAfter: choosing between isomeric starting materials by the carbon the group must sit on; writing a two-step route with an equation per step; building a four-reaction route from one starting material used in two roles; explaining a low overall yield; finding and correcting a wrong box and a wrong arrow in a given flow chart.
progression.nextLesson: addition polymers (route chem-m7-c14, "How does an alkene become an addition polymer?").

teaching.task: A synthesis question gives you a target and a short list of starting materials. How do you choose the start that puts each group on the right carbon, write every step with its conditions, and check a route for the box or arrow that quietly makes an isomer instead of the target?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why hex-3-ene: it is symmetrical, so the OH can only land on C3 (2b). Why hex-1-ene fails: water adds mainly to C2 (2b), and oxidation keeps the C=O where the OH was, so it makes an isomer (2d). Why the hydration arrow and the ester arrow get ⇌: both are equilibria (2c, 3c). Why the ketone stays: dichromate doesn't oxidise it further (2c). Why ethane needs chloroethane: no reaction met turns an alkane straight into an alcohol (3b). Why split the ethanol: the ester needs both the acid and the alcohol (3c, 3e). Why the yield is low: a mixture, an equilibrium, losses at several stages (3d). Why but-1-ene fails in Q3: mainly butan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol, gives a ketone dead end (4b). Why distillation fails: the aldehyde leaves before it is oxidised further (4c). Why 1-chlorobutane works: hydroxide takes the chlorine's place on the same carbon (4d). Why fixing only the arrow fails: reflux can't change which alcohol formed (4e).
teaching.conversationalApproach: A synthesis question gives a target and a short list of allowed starting materials, and the four moves from c13 (name and count, work backwards, choose, write forwards and check) still work, but exam questions hide their traps in the choice. Q1 (hexan-3-one from hex-1-ene or hex-3-ene) counts six carbons, needs hexan-3-ol, and chooses the symmetrical hex-3-ene so the OH can only land on carbon three, then writes hydration with a double arrow and dichromate oxidation under reflux; the classic slip makes hexan-2-one, an isomer. Q2 (ethyl ethanoate from ethane alone) works backwards from the ester cut, finds that both halves come from ethanol and that ethanol comes through chloroethane, then writes four reactions forwards with a split of the ethanol, and explains the low yield from the mixed chlorination, the esterification equilibrium and losses; the slip oxidises all the ethanol. Q3 (checking a plan for propyl butanoate) finds a wrong box, since but-1-ene gives mainly butan-2-ol and then butanone, and a wrong arrow, since distilling stops at the aldehyde, then rebuilds the route from 1-chlorobutane; the slip fixes only the arrow. A decision board closes: count carbons, choose the start that puts the group on the right carbon, split a shared start, and write every arrow with its conditions.
teaching.openingDecision: A synthesis question gives you a target and a short list of things you're allowed to start from. The four moves from the last video still work: name and count, work backwards, choose, then write forwards and check. But exam questions hide their traps in the choice: two starting materials that look almost the same, or a route that puts a group on the wrong carbon and makes an isomer of the target instead. Here are three HSC-style questions. Pause and try each one, then we'll work through it together.
teaching.understandingCheck: Three, each 10 s with the countdown and every demand and condition visible (2a, 3a, 4a): Q1's both alkenes and "two-step"; Q2's "only carbon-containing starting material" and "inorganic reagents may be used"; Q3's full student chart, the three available starting materials and "TWO errors". Nothing answer-bearing during the holds; the check strip dims.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, p56), as printed: "draft and construct flow charts to show reaction pathways for chemical synthesis, including those that involve more than one step" "write equations, state conditions and predict products to represent the reactions of alcohols, including but not limited to (ACSCH128, ACSCH136):" (listed examples: combustion, dehydration, substitution with HX, oxidation; G03 practises oxidation, with each step's equation in Q1) Practice and transfer only: first coverage stays with chem-m7-c13 (C7-IQ5-06) and chem-m7-c08a (C7-IQ4-04); G03 adds practice rows. starts at the route's "Read a target and allowed starting materials" and stops at its "Solve and check multi-step transformations and isomers". Three questions, each a chain with one trap: (1) hexan-3-one from hex-1-ene or hex-3-ene: choose the starting material by where the OH must sit, write a two-step flow chart with an equation per step (trap: hex-1-ene makes hexan-2-one, an isomer of the target); (2) ethyl ethanoate from ethane only: work backwards through the ester cut, go through a haloalkane, split the ethanol, then explain the low overall yield (trap: oxidising all the ethanol); (3) a student's flow chart for propyl butanoate with two errors, one in a box (but-1-ene gives mainly butan-2-ol, an isomer, which only reaches a ketone) and one on an arrow (distil instead of reflux): identify, explain, correct (trap: fixing only the arrow). Not here: the reaction map and the four moves themselves (c13, recalled in one clause each); mechanisms and Markovnikov's rule by name (c13 author note c; the narration says "mainly onto carbon two"); alcoholic NaOH elimination; reductions; yield calculations; purification detail (one grey chip "separate it" only); polymers (c14).

design.visualSystem: One practice board throughout, in the G02 layout: top-left the question card (stem, starting materials and demands, as an exam prints them, with the tag "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience"), kept readable through each question; the working fills the right two thirds; a type badge top-right ("Choose the start", "From one starting material", "Check a plan"), hidden during each attempt because it names the method. When the walkthrough starts, the card shrinks to a strip and each given is underlined in amber in the question text at the cue where it is used. A check strip on the far left carries four rows, "count carbons?", "group on the right carbon?", "conditions on every arrow?", "every box and arrow possible?", and ticks the row each scene uses; it dims to an outline during every countdown. Earlier questions are cleared before the next card writes on. Colour key from c13 and c08a: C=C teal, C–X orange-brown, OH ringed red, C=O and –COO– in navy; condition chips grey with the current arrow's chips bright; amber only for underlined givens and the path trace. Molecules are coded structural formulas in the c08a style. Clutter rule (owner): besides the question strip and the check strip, at most about three bright text items in the working area at once (a whole flow chart counts as one item once complete); completed arrows' chips dim while the current arrow writes; each tag fades when the next cue lands.
design.transitionPlan: The heading writes on and the c13 reaction map draws small and grey as four move cards light one at a time; each question opens on a fresh board with the type badge hidden while the worded card writes with its demands and answer boxes; the walkthrough shrinks the card to a strip, lights the type badge and underlines each given as it is used; the carbon ruler numbers the target and its C=O rings, the alkene models compare where the OH can land and the wrong one dims; the c13 flow chart builder runs left to right, each arrow's chips writing in spoken order; the ester cut slides the two halves apart and the backward chain writes; the yield funnel fans the chlorination into its mixture chips; the student's chart stays readable as a wrong box and then a wrong arrow ring and the corrected chart builds beside it; each question ends with its classic slip chip taking a red scribble cross; the check strip returns full size as a two-column board, each row lighting on its cue with its question badge; scene crossfade with settle.
